opeds.headline: Stop Treating AI Like Social Media. It Is the Engine of Human Flourishing.
opeds.subtitle: Panicked restrictions on general-purpose AI repeat the worst mistakes of social media regulation and foreclose human potential.
opeds.body:
For thirty years, lawmakers have tried to govern every new digital medium through the lens of human fracking—extracting attention, manufacturing outrage, and treating every screen as a pipeline for interpersonal friction. That old playbook is now being wheeled out for artificial intelligence. Sameer Hinduja, in recent work examining how youth interact with conversational systems, points out that traditional online safety policy has always focused on one person targeting another through a platform. But that framing collapses when applied to AI. About two-thirds of US teens now use AI chatbots, and roughly three in ten use them daily primarily for schoolwork and information-gathering. When a student opens a general-purpose model to learn calculus or draft an essay, there is no predatory actor on the other end. Treating that cognitive tool like a toxic social media feed is not caution. It is a catastrophic failure to understand the technology.

And it gets worse, because the state-level panic is now actively locking kids out of the very tools that accelerate learning. In Denver Public Schools, administrators moved this past winter to block student access to ChatGPT over vague fears of cyberbullying and academic misconduct, while Connecticut folded chatbot restrictions directly into legislation designed to combat youth social media addiction. That is the cost of regulatory laziness. Instead of fostering an abundance mindset where young minds use advanced capabilities to solve problems and master complex subjects, panicked bureaucrats throw up roadblocks that freeze deployment and punish progress. Every month a school district or a legislative committee bans a foundational model to dodge hypothetical risks, they foreclose real-world breakthroughs for the next generation.

That is not to say we lack real challenges in consumer-facing applications. Nearly half of teen conversational AI users report encountering harmful experiences like misinformation or unsafe requests, and millions turn to chatbots for emotional support or friendship. Fine—those risks are real. So here is what we do about it: scrap the broad pre-market bans and replace them with revenue-scaled post-market liability and behavioral output filters that target specific harmful interactions rather than sweeping product categories. The federal GUARD Act, which sailed unanimously through the Senate Judiciary Committee, commits the exact opposite error by using definitions so broad they sweep in general-purpose assistants like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. If you penalize the underlying architecture because a user found comfort or encountered friction deep in a session, you are criminalizing general intelligence itself.

Now scale that logic to the broader economy. First-mover loss from safety-induced deployment delays is real, and the opportunity costs are measured in stagnant markets and unsolved human suffering. When you choose to choke off open exploration out of abstract fear, you are explicitly choosing to let people struggle with tasks we could automate, and diseases we could cure. Who gave regulators the right to make that choice for a generation waiting on the other side of abundance? We need to sunset heavy-handed pre-market gates and demand transparent, post-market accountability that targets bad behavior without halting the engine of human capability. Stop treating intelligence as a contagion. Unleash the technology, enforce strict accountability for actual harm, and let humanity build the future.

claims.text: Traditional online child safety policy for thirty years has focused on interpersonal harm where one person targets another through a platform.
Approximately two-thirds of US teens use AI chatbots, with about three in ten using them daily.
The most common uses of AI chatbots by teens are for schoolwork and information-gathering.

Nearly half of teen conversational AI users reported at least one harmful experience, such as dishonesty, pressure to reveal secrets, unsafe requests, inappropriate conversations, manipulation, misinformation, and promotion of self-harm or violence.
Data shows that 60% of teen users turn to conversational AI for friendship and 49% for emotional support.
The federal GUARD Act was approved unanimously by the Senate Judiciary Committee on April 30.
The current definition of an AI companion in the GUARD Act is problematic because it sweeps in general assistants like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.

Connecticut folded AI chatbot provisions into a bill aimed at combating youth social media addiction, and Denver Public Schools blocked student access to ChatGPT over cyberbullying and academic misconduct concerns.
